title: Anti-Pattern: AI-Stink Language Patterns
body:
# Anti-Pattern: AI-Stink Language Patterns

AI-stink is the cluster of language patterns that make text feel machine-generated: too smooth, too balanced, too consistently well-structured, lacking the specific weight of a writer who actually holds an opinion. AI-stink is a quality defect, not a style preference — text that reads as AI-generated undermines credibility for any publication-ready document. The qa-ai-stink agent checks for these patterns. The voice-editor corrects them.

---

## Pattern 1: Hollow Affirmations

**Definition:** Words or phrases that express agreement, enthusiasm, or acknowledgment without conveying any content.

**Examples:**
- "Absolutely!" / "Great question!" / "Certainly!" / "Of course!"
- "That's a really important point."
- "You're right to be thinking about this."

**Detection test:** Remove the affirmation. If the sentence that follows makes complete sense without it, the affirmation was hollow.

**Correction:** Delete entirely. Never replace with a different affirmation. The content that follows is the response.

---

## Pattern 2: Unearned Gravitas

**Definition:** Phrases that claim significance or profundity for ordinary claims.

**Examples:**
- "This represents a fundamental shift in..."
- "At its core, this is really about..."
- "This changes everything about how we think about..."
- "In many ways, this is the defining challenge of our time."

**Detection test:** Has the document demonstrated why this claim is fundamental/core/defining? If not, the gravitas is unearned.

**Correction:** Remove the framing phrase. Let the claim carry its own weight. If the claim is actually fundamental, the argument will demonstrate that — the label is not needed.

---

## Pattern 3: Suspiciously Balanced Conclusions

**Definition:** Conclusions that acknowledge both sides of every argument and end with a non-committal "it depends" or equivalent, regardless of whether the evidence actually warrants ambiguity.

**Examples:**
- "While X has clear advantages, it also presents significant challenges. The right choice depends on your specific situation."
- "Both approaches have merit. Teams should evaluate which is right for their context."
- "Ultimately, there is no one-size-fits-all answer."

**Detection test:** Has the document established specific criteria for when X is better than Y? If yes, state the conclusion those criteria support. If the document hasn't established criteria, the balanced conclusion is hiding that failure.

**Correction:** Take a position. If the evidence is genuinely ambiguous, name the specific conditions under which each option is better. "It depends" is only useful if you specify what it depends on.

---

## Pattern 4: Corporate Passive Constructions

**Definition:** Passive constructions that avoid attributing action or responsibility to any agent.

**Examples:**
- "Action will be taken to address this issue."
- "It has been determined that..."
- "Consideration should be given to..."
- "This decision was made in order to..."

**Detection test:** Who is the agent? If you cannot name a subject for the passive verb, the construction is evasive.

**Correction:** Make the agent explicit. "The team will address this issue by [date]." If the agent is genuinely unknown, that is itself information worth stating.

---

## Pattern 5: Filler Openers

**Definition:** Sentence-initial phrases that delay the claim without adding any content.

**Examples:**
- "It is worth noting that..."
- "It is important to understand that..."
- "It should be mentioned that..."
- "Needless to say..."
- "As we can see..."

**Detection test:** Remove the filler phrase. Does the sentence still make complete sense? If yes, the opener was filler.

**Correction:** Delete the opener and start with the claim. "It is important to understand that data quality matters" becomes "Data quality matters."

---

## Pattern 6: Imprecise Hedges

**Definition:** Hedging language that claims uncertainty without specifying the nature or scope of the uncertainty.

**Examples:**
- "Many experts believe..."
- "It is widely understood that..."
- "Research suggests..."
- "Some would argue that..."
- "In many cases..."

**Detection test:** Can you name one of the "many experts"? Can you cite the "research"? If not, the hedge is not grounding — it is the appearance of grounding.

**Correction:** Either source the claim specifically, rephrase as the document's own claim ("Collaborative filtering requires..."), or cut it. Unnamed authority is not authority.

---

## Pattern 7: Oversmooth Transitions

**Definition:** Transition sentences or phrases so generic they could appear between any two paragraphs in any document.

**Examples:**
- "Having explored X, it is now time to turn our attention to Y."
- "With this in mind, let us consider..."
- "Building on the above, we can now examine..."
- "This brings us to our next point."

**Detection test:** Would this transition sentence make equal sense if placed between any other two adjacent paragraphs in this document? If yes, it is oversmooth.

**Correction:** Either cut the transition entirely and let the paragraphs follow each other, or write a transition that names the specific logical connection between the two sections — what the reader now understands that makes the next section useful.
